description: MilkyWays is a farmer-centered decision-support tool built for Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data. Using live NASA POWER 25-year agroclimatology alongside local soil type, acreage, and farmer-chosen priorities (soil health, water efficiency, heat resilience, feed quality, and waste-heat proximity), compares 4 candidate fodder crop rotations—including the farm's existing baseline—showing why each is suggested, its bare-field vulnerability window, synthetic nitrogen savings and key gaps.
summary: MilkyWays is a decision-support tool that ingests live NASA Earth observations to help an industrial dairy farm located next to an AI data centre decide what fodder crop rotation to plant next. Unlike generic crop calendars or black-box ML recommenders, our system pairs satellite climate, rainfall, and soil-moisture data with deterministic agronomic rules and dairy thermodynamics—testing growing-season heat stress, water balance, nitrogen-fixation cycles, and indirect waste-heat recovery without opaque guesswork. We built an end-to-end browser pipeline: fetching live NASA POWER agroclimatology data, combining it with GPM IMERG, SMAP, MODIS MOD13Q1, Landsat/HLS, and local soil profiles, scoring candidate fodder rotations against farmer-chosen priorities, and matching dairy plant thermal loads with closed-loop data centre waste heat. Results are presented in an interactive web interface with trade-off bars and an explicit double-wall heat-exchanger safety model ("the coolant never touches the milk"). This matters because dairy farms face shifting weather and high thermal energy demand (~70% thermal, ~30% electricity), while nearby data centres reject low-grade heat continuously; combining NASA open data in the field with circular heat in the plant cuts synthetic nitrogen fertiliser needs by 25–30% and turns wasted heat into safe pasteurisation and cold storage.
details:
MilkyWays is a web-based decision-support tool that combines NASA Earth observations, agronomic rotation rules, and dairy thermal engineering to guide fodder planting and waste-heat reuse for an industrial dairy farm located next to an AI data centre. The system queries the live NASA POWER Agroclimatology API directly in the browser for any farm coordinate, retrieving annual and monthly seasonal profiles for temperature (T2M, T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN), precipitation (PRECTOTCORR), solar irradiance (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN), and wind speed (WS2M). It pairs these observations with GPM IMERG rainfall onset timing, SMAP soil moisture, MODIS MOD13Q1 crop vigor, Landsat/HLS field-level reflectance, local soil texture, and farmer priority weights (Soil Health, Water Efficiency, Heat Resilience, and Dairy Feed Quality) to rank candidate rotations of energy silage (maize, sorghum) and nitrogen-fixing legumes (alfalfa, clover, cowpea, berseem). Alongside the field score, MilkyWays computes the dairy plant's daily thermal demand (~817 kWh/day for a 20,000 L/day reference plant) and models how low-grade data center waste heat (30–45 °C air or 55–70 °C liquid cooling) is boosted by a heat pump to 70–90 °C for HTST pasteurization (72–78 °C) and absorption chilling (~7.2 °C).

The benefits are transparency, agronomic validity, and food-safety clarity. Rather than relying on black-box machine learning predictions that farmers cannot verify, MilkyWays uses deterministic, explainable scoring with four mandatory domain checks (heat and solar PAR suitability, water and soil drainage balance, nitrogen-fixation cycle verification, and waste-heat temperature and isolation) and validates against explicit positive and negative controls—such as the commercial Gais, Switzerland mountain cheese dairy (1.5 GWh/year) and legume-cereal rotations (25–30% nitrogen fertilizer reduction) versus continuous maize monocropping and unboosted air waste heat. The intended impact is to give dairy operators a practical, zero-cost template to cut synthetic nitrogen fertilizer use, protect soil organic matter under shifting weather, and evaluate circular waste-heat recovery without compromising milk safety.

We built the project with HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript calling the live NASA POWER REST API directly in the browser, paired with Python, MkDocs Material for structured technical documentation, Mermaid.js for system and heat-loop diagrams, and GitHub Actions with GitHub Pages for zero-backend public deployment.

The project is creative because it bridges space-based Earth observation with a novel industrial symbiosis—cows and servers, milk and heat—linking what grows in the field to the thermal energy inside the dairy plant. We carefully considered real-world engineering and data limits, including NASA POWER's ~50 km grid resolution versus field-scale MODIS and Landsat layers, SMAP's 2015–present record length for current conditions only, the necessity of a heat-pump boost for pasteurization temperatures, and a closed-loop double-wall heat exchanger so data center coolant never touches the milk.
